Replacing first-generation turf in Reunion's earliest phases

Turf replacement in Reunion, tearing out a worn system and correcting the base before laying new material, prices close to a new install minus whatever base can be reused, quoted per job as of September 2026. Reunion's earliest phases, approved as a Development of Regional Impact back in 1992, are old enough now that some of the first turf lawns installed on those streets are reaching the end of a normal service life.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Housing age tells you where to look first

Osceola County has tracked Reunion Resort & Club of Orlando's buildout against a 2031 deadline since the county approved it as a Development of Regional Impact in 1992 osceola.org. That long a build-out window means Reunion's housing stock spans three decades of construction on the same property, and a turf system installed on one of the earliest streets not long after those first homes closed is a different replacement conversation than one installed five years ago on a newer section.

Picking a better-stabilized product for a lawn that wore out early

Turf generally lasts ten to twenty years depending on UV stabilization, traffic, and infill, and a Reunion lawn that wore out closer to the ten-year mark on a full-sun lot is a reasonable case for choosing a more UV-stable product the second time around rather than defaulting to the same specification. Spending a little more on stabilization during a replacement, when the labor and base work are already committed either way, is one of the more direct ways to push a new install toward the longer end of that lifespan range.

Say you have a first-generation lawn from an early phase

Say you have a 1,200 sq ft Reunion backyard on one of the resort's earliest streets, with turf that's showing matted, flattened fiber and a couple of lifted seams after years of use as part of a managed rental. Because the existing base checks out as still compacted and draining well, the replacement quote covers tearing out and disposing of the old surface, adjusting the base where it's settled unevenly, and laying new turf and infill, typically pricing at or slightly below what a ground-up install on the same footprint would run since the rock layer doesn't need rebuilding from scratch. A job like this usually finishes faster than a first-time install for the same reason, since a full day of demo, base repair and new turf replaces what would otherwise be a two-stage excavation and build process.

Why rental wear shortens the replacement clock

A turf lawn on a managed rental sees more concentrated foot traffic over its life than the same product would on an owner-occupied home used more lightly, simply because of how many different guest groups pass through a season, so the fiber can mat down and lose its upright look faster than the manufacturer's general lifespan estimate would suggest. That doesn't mean the base underneath needs rebuilding at the same pace; often the existing rock layer is still sound and only the surface and infill need replacing.

Old infill left mixed into a new install

Skipping a full infill removal during a Reunion replacement, especially where old crumb rubber or another synthetic infill was spread across a general lawn area, risks leaving that material mixed into the new build rather than confined to where it's actually allowed. A new installation that still has old rubber infill scattered through it hasn't actually corrected the mismatch it was supposed to fix, and it can be hard to tell from the surface that any of the old material is still present once new turf covers it.

A base that looks flat but was never washed to begin with

An older Reunion lawn's base can appear level and well-compacted on the surface while still holding a fines crust from subgrade material that was never washed before the original install, years before the current standard required it. That crust doesn't announce itself as a problem until the turf above it is pulled up during a replacement, at which point it's clear the base was never actually draining the way it looked like it was. Flat isn't the same as functional, which is why we check for a crust, not just for slope, before deciding a base can stay.

What gets reused and what doesn't

A replacement job starts with checking whether the existing washed crushed-rock base is still compacted, draining and free of the fines that would have bound it into a crust over time; if it's holding up, we build the new turf on top of it rather than tearing the base out along with the old surface, which is what keeps replacement priced below a full ground-up install. Irrigation heads capped under an older system usually stay capped, since the reason they were capped in the first place, the state's restriction on watering synthetic turf, hasn't changed.

Finding every irrigation head, not just the visible ones

An older Reunion lawn's sprinkler layout isn't always fully documented, so part of a replacement's process is running water to each zone before demo starts and flagging where heads actually sit, rather than relying on memory or an old irrigation plan that may not match what's actually in the ground. A head buried under years of turf and infill is easy to miss without this step, and finding it after the new base is already compacted means reopening finished work to cap a line that should have been caught earlier.

Keeping the new spec sheet for the next replacement cycle

The product spec sheet and invoice from a Reunion replacement are worth keeping somewhere easy to find, not just for an HOA that might ask again, but for whoever handles the next replacement ten to twenty years from now, since knowing exactly what backing, infill, and base depth went in saves a round of guessing when that lawn eventually needs the same decision made again. A folder with the paperwork from this job is a small thing that saves real time on the next one.

Questions people ask

How do I know if my Reunion turf needs full replacement or just a repair?

A few loose seams or a small worn patch usually points to a repair visit; widespread matting, a base that's stopped draining, or fiber that's lost its upright feel across most of the yard points to replacement. See the turf replacement page for the signs we look for.

Does replacing turf on an older Reunion lot need a new association submittal?

Often a lighter one than a first-time install, since the yard's overall look isn't changing, but it's worth checking with the resort's property owners association before assuming a straightforward swap needs no paperwork at all.
